text: Day one. You wake up, walk downstairs, and there's a number floating above your mom's head. One hundred.
Morning, sweetheart! Pancakes?
Above your dad: one hundred.|Above your little sister, who put a frog in your shoe last week: also one hundred.
Benny, you have syrup on your face.
You don't know what the numbers mean yet.|But you're about to find out.|At school.|The hard way.
So... what if you could see how much everyone likes you?
The hallway is a sea of numbers. Twelve. Forty-five. Zero. A kid you've never even met: zero. Fair.
Ben! Did you finish the science homework? I need to copy... I mean, compare.
Your best friend since kindergarten. Sixty-two. Not bad. Not great. Kind of... a C minus.
And then Lila walks past.|The girl who plays violin at every school concert.|The girl you've liked since fourth grade.
Three. Three percent. You've seen higher numbers above the vending machine.
Ben! Homework, please. And try to stay awake today.

Mister Hale: forty-eight.|Basically a coin flip.|A red-haired kid in a green sweater walks past, staring at everyone's eyes like he can hear something.|Weird.|His number for you?|Fifty.|Strangers are generous.
You. New kid who sits by the window.
I've been here for three years.
...Cool jacket.
Dex.|The kid teachers walk around in the hallway.|Ninety-one.|Ninety-one percent.|Dex likes you more than your best friend does.
You have no idea what to do with that information.|So you do what anyone would do.|You say "thanks" and run.
That night you lie in bed doing math.|Mom, one hundred.|Dex, ninety-one.|Theo, sixty-two.|Lila, three.|Somewhere in that list is a lesson.|You just can't read it yet.
By day three, you start taking notes.|Rule one: the numbers only change when something happens between you and that person.
You held a door for a teacher.|Plus four.|You laughed at a joke that wasn't funny.|Minus two.|People can tell.
Rule two: you can't see your own number.|Not in the mirror, not in a window, not in a spoon.|You checked.|Twice.
Rule three: the numbers never lie. Which is great. Until it isn't.
You test it on your mom.|You do the dishes without being asked.|Still one hundred.|You leave your socks on the stairs.|Still one hundred.|Moms are broken.|In the best way.
Day seven. The popular kids wave you over. Their numbers are low, but their table is shiny.
Hey, I saved you a seat! I brought the good chips!
Oh , sorry, man. Tomorrow?
Fifty-five.|You watch it happen.|You watch your best friend like you a little bit less, in real time.
The worst part? He still waves at you from across the room. Fifty-four.
And the popular kids?|Their numbers don't move at all.|Fourteen, eleven, nine.|You traded a sixty-two for a table full of single digits.
Day nine.|You decide to fix Lila's number.|You watch three videos called "How to make anyone like you." You practise in the mirror.
Hey. Your violin... is very... shiny. Like your... hair. Which is also... nice.
...Thanks? I have to go.
One percent. You actually made it go DOWN. People can feel when you're trying too hard.
You walk home holding a rose nobody wanted.|A dog on the street looks at you.|No number.|Dogs like everybody.|You need that energy.
Here's the thing. Most people are terrible at guessing how much others like them.
In a study at Cornell and Yale, strangers talked for five minutes, then guessed how much the other person liked them.|Almost everyone guessed too low.
Scientists call it the liking gap.|People like us more than we think.|You're the only person on Earth who can see the real number.|And it still doesn't help.
Day twelve. You give up on speeches. You just say hi to Lila every morning. That's it. Hi.
Four. Then nine. Then fifteen. Not because hi is magic. Because you keep showing up.
Psychologists noticed this in 1968: the more often we see someone, the more we tend to like them.|They call it the mere exposure effect.
In one classroom study, a student who simply showed up to more lectures was rated more likable , by people who never even talked to her.
Day fifteen. Dex's backpack rips open in the hallway. Everybody laughs. You don't even think. You just help.
Two years ago, you were the only kid who didn't laugh when I tripped in gym.|You probably don't remember.
You don't. But he did. For two whole years. Ninety-four.
Sometimes you have no idea which tiny moment someone will remember forever.
Day eighteen. Theo's number is forty-one. You've been so busy watching numbers that you stopped watching your friend.
I brought the good chips. And I'm sorry. For the seat. And the rest.
...Took you long enough. You're player two.
Sixty. Seventy-five. Eighty-eight. You don't even notice when it hits ninety. You're too busy losing at video games.
There's a reason this works: we tend to like the people who show they like us.|Psychologists call it reciprocity.|Theo just calls it Tuesday.
Day twenty-two.|Lila's solo at the winter concert.|Halfway through, her bow slips.|One horrible squeak.|The whole room goes quiet.
You do the only thing you can think of.|You stand up.|And you clap.|Loud.|Alone.|For about three very long seconds.
Then Theo stands up. Then Dex. Then the whole room.
That was the worst concert of my life. Thank you for making it the best.
Sixty-seven. Not a hundred. And somehow, that feels better than a hundred ever could.
Is this seat taken? The good chips table, right?
Only for people who clap at concerts.
Seventy-two.|She sits with you every day after that.|You never tell her about the numbers.|Some things are better without a score.
Day twenty-five. Bad day. Zoe spills juice on your science project and you yell. Really yell.
I'm sorry, Benny. I just wanted to help.
You look up, ready to watch her number crash. One hundred. It doesn't even flicker.
Some people's numbers aren't about what you do.|They're about who you are to them.|You spend the rest of the night helping her fix the drawing.
You know she thinks you're a superhero, right?
You do now. You can literally see it.
Day thirty.|Midnight.|You brush your teeth, look in the mirror, and for the first time there's a number above your own head.
Forty-one. Lower than Dex. Lower than Lila. Lower than the hamster's best friend.
And you realise what it means. Not how much others like you. How much YOU like you.
Okay. Let's work on that one.
Forty-two.
Thirty days of numbers taught you three things.|People like you more than you think.|Showing up beats showing off.|And being kind to yourself counts too.
Day thirty-one. You walk downstairs. No numbers. Just your family, and pancakes.
Benny, you have syrup on your face. Again.
You can't see how much they like you anymore. But for the first time, you don't need to.
At school, Theo saves you a seat.|Dex nods at you in the hallway.|Lila waves with her violin case.|No numbers.|Just people.|Your people.
If you could see one person's number, whose would you look at first? Tell me in the comments.
